lines.note: `cujǒ ſuru` mechanically gives クジョウ スル. The Portuguese says “to manifest or confess openly”; this line begins a continuation from the preceding page, so the missing lexical context should not be reconstructed here.
This completes Portuguese `abertamente`, “openly.” The physical line contains no Japanese, but it confirms the sense of the preceding verbal phrase.
`Facujù` gives ハクジュウ and corresponds naturally to 百獣, literally “the hundred beasts.” Portuguese `cem animaes` is “a hundred animals.”

runs.text: Certa aruore que tem as fo-

lines.note: `Facuju` gives ハクジュ, while `Cayano qi` is カヤノ キ, “kaya tree.” The Portuguese begins “a certain tree whose leaves…,” identifying the entry by description rather than translation.
This completes “whose leaves are like those of a cypress.” Historical `acipreſte` corresponds to modern Portuguese `cipreste`.
`Facuma` gives ハクマ; `Cami` is カミ, “paper.” Editorial `i,` means “that is,” and should not itself receive a kana reading. Portuguese `papel` confirms the meaning.
`Facumai` is ハクマイ, 白米. `Xirozzuqino come` gives シロズキノ コメ, roughly “white/polished rice”; `come` is historical Japanese *kome*, not Portuguese “eat.”
Portuguese `arroz branco, ou pilado` means “white or pounded/polished rice,” confirming the Japanese explanation on the preceding line.
`Facumei` gives ハクメイ and `Aqiraca` is アキラカ, modern 明らか. The compound may evoke modern 明白 with the elements reversed. Historical `euidencia` is modern Portuguese `evidência`.
The same spelling `Facumei` here denotes ハクメイ in the sense 薄命, “short-lived” or “an early death,” as the Portuguese “short life, of little duration” makes clear.

`Facuracu` gives ハクラク, naturally 伯楽, a judge or healer of horses. Historical Portuguese `Alueitar` corresponds to modern `alveitar`, a farrier or veterinary practitioner, and supports that identification.
`Facuran` is ハクラン, naturally 博覧. `Firoqu miru` is ヒロク ミル, literally “to see/read broadly.” Portuguese begins “great study or learning.”
Portuguese `letras` here means learning or letters. `Facuranno fito` is ハクランノ ヒト, “a person of broad learning”; `Homẽ de grã-` continues as “a man of great…”.
This completes `Homẽ de grãde estudo, & letras`, “a man of great study and learning.” The split `grã- / de` is purely physical line division.
This `Facuran` is the disease ハクラン rather than 博覧. Portuguese `mordexim` is an early modern disease term; the note says that the proper word follows.
`Quacuran` should be read クヮクラン, with historical labialized `qua`; this corresponds to 霍乱. Portuguese `a propria palaura he` means “the proper word is.”
`Facurǒ` is ハクロウ and `Xiranami` is シラナミ, “white waves.” Portuguese describes waves white with foam.
This completes the image: waves “which break with foam.” Historical `quebrão` corresponds to modern `quebram`.
`Facuro` is ハクロ and `Xiraſagui` is シラサギ, modern 白鷺. In `gui`, the `u` is orthographic and silent; Portuguese `garça branca` is “white heron/egret.”
`Facuro` is ハクロ and `Xiratçuyu` is シラツユ, 白露. Historical Portuguese `orualho` is modern `orvalho`, “dew.”
`Facurǒ` is ハクロウ; `Fiacuno xinrǒ` reads ヒャクノ シンロウ, 百の辛労, “a hundred hardships.” Portuguese `muitos trabalhos` confirms “many labors/troubles.”

runs.text: Hũ paſſarinho que tem o bico

lines.note: `Facurǒ` is ハクロウ, here equated with `mozu` モズ, the shrike. Portuguese begins “a little bird which has the beak…”.

The bird’s beak is compared with a falcon’s. `S.` is a source or register abbreviation. `Facuro nhôjet` is visibly difficult and should remain an unresolved printed form rather than be normalized from expectation.
Ignoring editorial `i,`, `Mozuno ſayezzuru coto` gives モズノ サエズル コト, “the shrike’s singing/chirping.” Portuguese begins “the singing of this…”.
This completes `O cantar eſte paſſarinho`, “the song of this little bird.” The missing `d` in what modern Portuguese would write `deste` is part of the printed historical text.
`Facuſa` gives ハクサ. Portuguese means “disease of the teeth”; the exact kanji or medical identification is not safely recoverable from this line alone.
`Facuſui` is ハクスイ, naturally 白水. Historical `Agoa clara` is modern `água clara`, “clear water.”
`Facutô` is ハクトウ; `Xiroi caxira` is シロイ カシラ, “white head,” and `Xiraga` is シラガ, gray/white hair. Portuguese `Caãs` is an old spelling of `cãs`, gray hairs.
`Facutôni voyobu` reads ハクトウニ オヨブ, literally “to reach/come to white-headedness.” Portuguese `Fazerſe branco` means “to become white”; the editorial `i,` introduces the next synonym.
Portuguese `velho` supplies the extended sense “old.” `S.` is an editorial abbreviation and not Japanese.
`Facutǒ` is ハクトウ; `Xiroi momo` is シロイ モモ, “white peach.” Portuguese begins “white peach blossom.”
This completes historical `peſegueiro`, modern Portuguese `pessegueiro`, “peach tree.”
`Facutocu` is ハクトク; `Firoi toku` is ヒロイ トク, “broad/great benefit.” Historical `proueitos` is modern `proveitos`, “benefits.”
`Xeqigacuniua facutocu nari` reads セキガクニワ ハクトク ナリ. Here `niua` represents the particle sequence には and is pronounced ニワ. `Vt` introduces the example.

runs.text: continuo, & grãde estudo ha grãdes proueitos.

lines.note: The Portuguese paraphrase says that continual and great study brings great benefits. `grãde/grãdes` are printed historical spellings of modern `grande/grandes`.
`Facuvn` reads ハクウン: final-context `v` represents vocalic `u`, giving 白雲. `Xiroi cumo` is シロイ クモ, and historical `Nuuem branca` is modern `nuvem branca`, “white cloud.”
`Facuuô` gives ハクオウ and `Camome` is カモメ. Historical Portuguese `Gaiuotas` is modern `gaivotas`, “seagulls.”
`Facuxa` is ハクシャ; `Xiroi iſago` is シロイ イサゴ, “white sand/gravel.” Portuguese begins “small white stones of the…”.
This completes `Pedrinhas brancas da praya`, modern `pedrinhas brancas da praia`, “little white stones from the beach.”
`Facuxei` is ハクセイ and `Fiacuxǒ` is ヒャクショウ, modern 百姓. Portuguese begins “farmer or rustic…”.
This completes `Laurador, ou ruſtico do campo`, modern `lavrador, ou rústico do campo`: “farmer, or country rustic.”
`Facuxen` is ハクセン; `Xiroi xiqimono` is シロイ シキモノ, “white spread/covering.” Portuguese offers “felt, or another…”.
This completes “cloth of white wool.” Historical `laã` represents modern Portuguese `lã`.
`Facuxeqi` is ハクセキ, naturally 白石; `Xiroi ixi` is シロイ イシ. Portuguese `Pedra branca` gives the same literal meaning, “white stone.”
`Facuxet` gives ハクセツ, naturally 白雪; `Xiroi yuqi` is シロイ ユキ. Historical Portuguese `Neue` is modern `neve`, “snow.”
`Facuxi` is ハクシ, naturally 白紙; `Xiroi cami` is シロイ カミ. Portuguese `Papel branco` means “white paper.”
The same `Facuxi` spelling here is explained by `Vſui cami`, ウスイ カミ, “thin paper.” Portuguese `Papel fino` confirms that this is a different sense from the preceding white-paper entry.

runs.text: Facuxu. Xiroi ſaqe. i, Nigori ſaqe.

lines.note: `Facuxu` is ハクシュ; `Xiroi ſaqe` is シロイ サケ and `Nigori ſaqe` is ニゴリ サケ. Portuguese begins a description of white, cloudy Japanese wine/sake.
This completes `Vinho branco turuo de Iapão`, modern `vinho branco turvo do Japão`, “cloudy white wine of Japan.”

runs.text: Caſa, onde ſe vendem folhas dou-

lines.note: `Facuya` gives ハクヤ. Portuguese begins “a house where sheets/leaves of gold or silver are sold,” suggesting a trade name rather than an ordinary house.
This completes `folhas douro, ou de prata`, modern `folhas de ouro, ou de prata`, “gold or silver leaf.”
`Facuye` is ハクエ and `Vſui qirumono` is ウスイ キルモノ, “thin clothing.” Portuguese begins “lightly clothed, or…”.
This completes Portuguese `Pouco vestido, ou ſingello`, “lightly/simply dressed.” Historical `ſingello` corresponds to modern `singelo`.
`Facuye` again gives ハクエ; `Xiroi coromo` is シロイ コロモ, “white robe.” Portuguese begins “a white garment of thin…”.
This completes `ſeda delgada`, “thin/fine silk.”
`Vſuguinu` is ウスギヌ, 薄衣/薄絹, a thin silk fabric or garment. Portuguese `Peça delgada de ſeda` confirms “a thin piece of silk.”
`Facuyô` is ハクヨウ and `Xiroi fitçuji` is シロイ ヒツジ. Historical Portuguese `Ouelha branca` is modern `ovelha branca`, “white sheep.”
`Fada` is ハダ, modern 肌; `Fadaye` is ハダエ, 肌え/肌. Portuguese begins “the surface of the flesh, or the human…”.
The definition completes as “human body.” `Fadauo yuruſu` is ハダヲ ユルス; Portuguese begins `Deſcuidarſe`, “to let oneself become careless.”
`Melius` is Latin “better,” recommending `Cocorouo yuruſu` ココロヲ ユルス as the preferable expression. The final `Fa-` begins a Japanese continuation across the physical line.

Joined with the preceding fragment, `Fadato fadauo auaſuru` reads ハダト ハダヲ アワスル, literally “to bring body/skin together with body/skin.” Portuguese begins a sexual euphemism, “for the man to have union…”.
Portuguese completes “the man with a woman.” Historical `molher` corresponds to modern `mulher`. `Fadauo a-` begins another occurrence of the Japanese phrase across the line break.

runs.text: ſe diz dos que ſe unem, & eſtão ami-

lines.note: `Fadauo auaſuru` is ハダヲ アワスル. Portuguese says it is used of people who unite and are friendly; the physical split `ami-` continues to `gos`.

runs.text: gos, mas não he muito vſado nem proprio.

lines.note: This completes the usage warning: it may describe people who are close friends, but “it is not much used nor proper.”
`Fadabacama` is ハダバカマ, literally “skin/body hakama.” Portuguese identifies inner breeches comparable to drawers.
This completes historical Portuguese `ciroulas`, drawers or under-breeches.

runs.text: Fortaleza nua. i, Sem vallos, nẽ

lines.note: `Fadacajiro` is ハダカジロ, 裸城, literally “naked castle.” Portuguese explains a bare fortress without ditches or walls.
This completes `Sem vallos, nẽ muros`, modern `sem valos, nem muros`, “without ditches or walls.”
`Fadacajironi` is ハダカジロニ, the adverbial form “as a bare/defenseless castle.” `Adu.` marks an adverb and `Vt` introduces the example; `nat-` continues to `ta`.

runs.text: Ficou a fortaleza desbaratada ſem muros,

lines.note: Together `Fadacajironi natta` is ハダカジロニ ナッタ, “it became a bare castle.” Portuguese says the fortress was left dismantled and without walls.
This completes the Portuguese example with `vallos`, modern `valos`, “ditches.”
`Fadacana` is ハダカナ, modern 裸な. Portuguese `Eſtar nũ, ou deſpido` means “to be naked or undressed.”
`Fadacani` is ハダカニ, “nakedly/in a naked state.” `Fadacani naru` is ハダカニ ナル, “to become naked”; Portuguese begins the same definition.
`Fadacani naſu` is ハダカニ ナス, causative in sense: “to make another naked.” Portuguese `Deſpir a outro` means “to undress another.”
Portuguese adds “completely,” then a further sense “to rob and strip him.” `Roubalo` and `deſpojallo` reflect clitic spellings now written `roubá-lo` and `despojá-lo`.

runs.text: Camiſa ao modo de Iapão aber-

lines.note: `Fadacatabira` is ハダカタビラ, modern 肌帷子, an undergarment. Portuguese begins “a shirt in the Japanese fashion, open…”.

runs.text: ta por diante branca, ou de outras cores.

lines.note: This completes the description: open at the front, white or of other colors.
`Fadaca vma` is ハダカ ウマ, “bare horse,” meaning an unsaddled horse. Portuguese `Caualo em oſſo` conveys riding without saddle or padding.
`Fadaca vmani vchinoru` is ハダカ ウマニ ウチノル, “to mount/ride a bare horse.” Portuguese repeats “to ride the horse bareback.”

runs.text: Vestido junto à carne que ordinaria-

lines.note: `Fadagui` is ハダギ, modern 肌着, clothing worn directly against the skin. Portuguese begins precisely that definition.
This completes “which ordinarily is `Auaxe`.” `Auaxe` is a Japanese garment/fabric term retained in roman type within the Portuguese explanation.
`Fadaqe` is ハダケ. Portuguese defines the space between a bow and its string; the precise modern lexical equivalent is less obvious than the kana reading.
`Fadaqe, uru, eta` represents ハダケル with its inflectional forms. Portuguese `Almofaçar o caualo` refers to grooming/rubbing a horse; `Vt` introduces examples.
`Vmauo fadaquru` reads ウマヲ ハダクル and applies the verb to a horse. `Fitouo nade fada-` begins a second example, “stroking a person…”.

runs.text: Tratar a alguem com mimos, & a-

lines.note: Completing `Fitouo nade fadaquru`, the Japanese is ヒトヲ ナデ ハダクル. Portuguese explains “to treat someone with caresses and…”.
This completes Portuguese `afagos`, “caresses/fondling.”
`Fadaqegatana` is ハダケガタナ, apparently the implement associated with grooming horses. Portuguese `almofaça` is a currycomb or grooming tool.
`Fadareni` is ハダレニ. `Fadareni furu yuqi` is ハダレニ フル ユキ and introduces a description of the way fallen snow weighs on vegetation.

runs.text: do de eſtarem as folhas das aruores, ou eruas

lines.note: Portuguese describes “the manner in which leaves of trees or grasses are…”. Historical `aruores` and `eruas` correspond to modern `árvores` and `ervas`.

runs.text: inclinadas com a neue que cabio.

lines.note: This completes the image: leaves bent down by the snow that has fallen. Historical `neue` and `cabio` correspond to modern `neve` and `caiu`.
`Fadauobi` is ハダオビ, modern 肌帯, glossed as a close-fitting band or setting. `Fadauobiuo ſuru` reads ハダオビヲ スル, “to put on/use a hadaobi.”
Portuguese `Encaſtarſe`, modern `encastar-se`, supplies the verbal sense “to fit or set oneself closely.”
`Fadaxi` is ハダシ, modern 裸足. Portuguese `Deſcalço` is modern `descalço`, “barefoot”; `Fadaxini ayumu` is ハダシニ アユム.
This completes the example’s Portuguese translation, “to walk with bare feet.” Modern spelling would accent `pés`.
